clinicalPearls: Each traditional morphologic form of cardiomyopathy (hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive) can be caused or modified by underlying genetic factors; heritability is well recognized in HCM and present in at least 30% of dilated cardiomyopathy without another clear etiology (p.2003-2004).

Most familial cardiomyopathies are autosomal dominant, with occasional autosomal recessive, matrilineal (mitochondrial), and X-linked inheritance; missense and truncating variants are the commonest abnormalities (p.2003).

Genetic cardiomyopathy shows age-dependent and incomplete penetrance: the phenotype is rarely present at birth and in some carriers may never manifest; relatives carrying the same variant can differ markedly in severity and progression (p.2004).
Penetrance and clinical severity tend to be greater in men for most cardiomyopathies; current therapy is based on phenotype rather than the genetic defect (p.2004).

The greatest current utility of genetic testing is to focus and inform family evaluations; it can also provide risk stratification and occasionally identify a treatable disorder such as Fabry's or Gaucher's disease (p.2004).

A sarcomere gene variant is found in roughly 40-50% of HCM patients, more often with familial disease and asymmetric septal hypertrophy; about 80% of these involve MYH7 or MYBPC3 encoding the thick myofilament (p.2005).

HCM is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy developing without a causative hemodynamic factor (e.g., hypertension, aortic valve disease) or infiltrative/storage disease; prevalence is about 1:500 (p.2005).

Outflow tract obstruction is present at rest in about 30% of HCM patients and provoked by exercise in another ~30%; systolic anterior motion of an enlarged anterior mitral leaflet against the hypertrophied septum produces obstruction and posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation (p.2006).

Truncating variants in TTN (titin) are the commonest genetic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, accounting for up to 25% of familial DCM; men with TTN truncating variants typically develop disease about a decade before women (p.2008-2009).

DCM is considered present when LVEF is <=0.50 and/or LV diastolic dimension exceeds the 95th percentile predicted for age and sex; some patients have reduced LVEF with minimal dilation (nondilated/minimally dilated cardiomyopathy) (p.2008).

Inherited metabolic and storage disorders can mimic HCM by thickening the myocardium with abnormal products ('pseudohypertrophy'), classically with a short PR interval; most are diagnosed in childhood (p.2010).

Fabry's disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency from GLA variants) can affect female carriers; endomyocardial biopsy shows diagnostic concentric lamellar inclusions on electron microscopy, and diagnosis matters because enzyme replacement can reduce deposits (p.2010).
harrison.pathophysiology: Many distinct genes are implicated (locus heterogeneity), each with numerous pathogenic variants (allelic heterogeneity). Mutant proteins can interfere with the normal allele via a dominant-negative mechanism, while nonsense/frameshift variants may yield truncated or unstable proteins whose absence causes disease through haploinsufficiency; some genetic DCM combines both effects. Functional gene groups include sarcomeric proteins, Z-disk/cytoskeletal proteins, nuclear membrane proteins, excitation-contraction coupling proteins, metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial DNA, sarcolemmal membrane proteins, and desmosomal proteins. In HCM, sarcomere variants enhance calcium sensitivity, maximal force generation, and ATPase activity, producing abnormal energetics and impaired relaxation; myofibril and myocyte misalignment/disarray occurs, with interstitial fibrosis appearing before overt hypertrophy and focal replacement fibrosis providing arrhythmic substrate, plus microvascular ischemia from thickened intramural vessels. In DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, cytoskeletal, sarcolemmal (dystrophin), nuclear membrane (lamin A/C, emerin), and desmosomal protein defects impair force transmission, mechanical/electrical coupling, and cell survival; desmosomal disruption activates Wnt/beta-catenin and proinflammatory signaling with replacement of myocytes by fat and fibrous tissue, creating arrhythmogenic, sometimes aneurysmal regions.
additionalDifferentials: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy / arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
Restrictive cardiomyopathy (inherited, including DES-related and transthyretin amyloidosis)
Conduction disease with dilated cardiomyopathy (e.g., LMNA, SCN5A)
Inherited metabolic/storage cardiomyopathies (Fabry's, Danon, PRKAG2, carnitine and fatty-acid oxidation defects, mitochondrial syndromes)
nonInfectiousMimics: Athlete's heart (physiologic hypertrophy that regresses with detraining, with supernormal VO2max >50 mL/kg/min, mild dilation, and normal diastolic function)
Hypertensive or aortic valve disease causing secondary LV hypertrophy
Infiltrative/storage disease mimicking HCM via pseudohypertrophy (often with short PR interval)
Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-variant amyloid causing restrictive physiology
additionalInvestigations: Detailed multigenerational family history (heart failure, cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, conduction disease, tachyarrhythmias, sudden death, early atrial fibrillation/pacemaker, muscular dystrophy)
Two-dimensional and Doppler echocardiography (central to HCM/DCM diagnosis; physical exam and ECG are insensitive for HCM)
Cardiac MRI for myocardial fibrosis (late gadolinium enhancement) and inflammation
Genetic counseling and multigene cardiomyopathy panel testing, with confirmatory variant testing in relatives

Endomyocardial biopsy with electron microscopy when a specific diagnosis with therapeutic implications is suspected (e.g., Fabry's lamellar inclusions; not used to diagnose HCM but can exclude infiltrative/metabolic disease)
Enzyme activity assay and/or GLA sequencing when Fabry's disease suspected
Ambulatory ECG monitoring and exercise testing for nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and outflow gradient provocation
redFlags: History of cardiac arrest or spontaneous sustained ventricular tachycardia
Syncope, particularly nonvagal and occurring with or after exertion
Family history of sudden cardiac death at early ages
LV systolic dysfunction with ejection fraction <50% in HCM
LV apical aneurysm (especially with apical hypertrophy)
Spontaneous nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (>3 beats at rate >120)
High late gadolinium enhancement burden on cardiac MRI
Pathogenic LMNA or FLNC variants, or right-ventricular cardiomyopathy progressing to LV dysfunction (higher arrhythmic/adverse-event risk)
harrison.prognosis: HCM prognosis is better than in early referral-population studies but mortality remains higher than in age-matched individuals without cardiomyopathy; sudden death risk is under 1% per year (about 0.5% per year baseline). Up to 1 in 20 HCM patients progress to overt systolic dysfunction (EF <50%) with or without dilation ('burned out'/end-stage HCM), with increased risk of death from progressive heart failure and sudden death unless transplanted. In DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, prognosis is driven by disease stage and sudden-death risk, which is higher for variants in DES, DSP, DSC2, FLNC, LMNA, PKP2, PLN, RBM20, SCN5A, and TMEM43; progression rate is also gene-dependent, and patients with TTN truncating variants frequently recover with medical therapy.
pitfalls: Identifying a variant in a proband to focus family screening requires high certainty the variant is truly pathogenic and not a benign DNA variant.

Most identified variants are 'private' to individual families, complicating interpretation; growing recognition that multiple intermediate-effect alleles and polygenic risk influence penetrance and expression.
Athlete's heart can mimic mild HCM; distinguishing features include regression with detraining, supernormal exercise capacity, mild dilation, and normal diastolic function.
Late gadolinium enhancement on MRI, once attributed to prior viral myocarditis, is now recognized as common in genetic cardiomyopathy.
Cardiac glycosides should be avoided in HCM with obstruction because they increase contractility and worsen obstruction.
The positive predictive value of most HCM sudden-death risk factors is low, so many patients receiving a defibrillator never receive appropriate device therapy.
Endomyocardial biopsy is not used to diagnose HCM itself but may exclude infiltrative/metabolic disease.
harrison.severityClassification: HCM sudden-death risk stratification uses major risk factors (prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT, exertional/nonvagal syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, LV apical aneurysm, maximal wall thickness >30 mm, LVEF <50%) plus modifying factors (late gadolinium enhancement burden, spontaneous nonsustained VT). The externally validated European Society of Cardiology HCM Risk-SCD calculator integrates age, LV outflow tract gradient, left atrial diameter, maximal wall thickness, syncope, family history, and nonsustained VT to estimate 5-year cardiac-arrest risk: ICD generally advised at >=6%, considered at 4-6%, and not advised at <4%. DCM is defined by LVEF <=0.50 and/or LV diastolic dimension >95th percentile for age and sex.
management: Phenotype-directed therapy, since treatment currently follows the morphological picture rather than the specific gene defect

For dilated cardiomyopathy, guideline-directed heart failure therapy with beta-blockers, renin-angiotensin inhibitors or an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist

For hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, disopyramide and a cardiac myosin inhibitor such as mavacamten for obstruction, with septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation for refractory obstruction
Sudden cardiac death risk stratification with implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement in high-risk individuals, and anticoagulation when atrial fibrillation develops
Identify treatable phenocopies such as Fabry disease for enzyme replacement, and manage arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with antiarrhythmics and strict exercise restriction
Lifestyle advice including avoidance of competitive or high-intensity sport and of dehydration in obstructive hypertrophic disease
Genetic counselling with multigene panel testing of the proband and cascade clinical and genetic screening of relatives
Escalate to advanced heart failure therapies including transplantation or mechanical circulatory support for end-stage disease
